source.title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and figure labels are imperfectly rendered, but the main results and text descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and empirically checks scaling in a toy language-prediction model, but uses normalized squared-loss regret and varies embedding width and vocabulary size rather than testing the claim versions’ held-out cross-entropy or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports capacity-versus-regret results for a random-features bigram model. These bear on scaling-law behavior generally, but do not measure the specific outcomes named in V1–V7: in particular, regret is relative to an unconstrained empirical optimum, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, and there is no compute-budget allocation experiment.
record.test_reason: This is a toy-model theory paper: a fixed random-feature linear bigram, with in-sample squared-loss regret against the unconstrained empirical optimum, as width N varies. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss of language models against parameters, tokens or compute. It also has no compute allocation, architecture-shape, extrapolation or downstream results. It offers a mechanism and claims to recover the Kaplan functional form, but its results do not bear on whether any V1–V7 version holds for LMs. The record's 'tests/T2' conflicts with its own all-'not_tested' version list.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say the random-embedding bottleneck isolates capacity-driven scaling, and that the theory 'recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws' in the appropriate regime. They suggest heavy-tailed token statistics may underlie both capacity- and optimization-driven scaling, and report that experiments closely match the predicted curves. They frame the bigram model as a testbed 'without equating them with full transformers'.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a fixed random-feature bottleneck in a bigram model, optimizes the predictor, and measures normalized squared-loss regret against an unconstrained empirical optimum. It varies embedding width and vocabulary size, rather than measuring held-out transformer cross-entropy across parameter, token, or compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived regret laws vary across Zipf-exponent regimes and between sublinear and linear width regimes; the finite-sample contribution also depends on vocabulary occupancy and sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: In a fixed-random-embedding bigram model, optimal-predictor regret follows explicit laws by Zipf regime. For α<1 at sublinear width there is a constant floor (B≃A); at α=1 it falls logarithmically; for α>1 it follows N^−(α−1). A finite-sample term (1−A)d/n is added. WikiText-2 and OpenWebText2 sweeps reportedly match the theory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational-bottleneck regret in a Zipfian bigram model scales with width in a way set by the Zipf exponent; only the supercritical regime gives a pure power law in N.

record.problems: The evidence is from an analytically tractable bigram toy model with fixed random embeddings, not full language models. The empirical outcome is normalized squared-loss regret rather than held-out cross-entropy. Experimental values are presented in plots without exact numbers in the text; variability is shown but not numerically reported. The theorem relies on Zipf and constant-collision assumptions and a stated large-sample condition.

untested.parts: All: no held-out LM pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All. Top-k accuracy is mentioned but not reported.

record.verdict_notes: Synthetic-data experiments are mentioned but no figure or result is shown. The paper's statement that subcritical and critical laws 'better match' Kaplan is asserted, not shown against LM data. Relation is downgraded from the record's 'tests/T2' because no LM loss result bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or compute when the other resources are not bottlenecks.
Whether fits from small runs predict losses of much larger runs.
The loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation under a fixed compute budget and its scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted language-model loss exponents and compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices or training setup; departures of those loss curves from a single power law.

rows.subject: capacity-constrained bigram model with fixed random embeddings
rows.size_stated: Embedding width N; Nd trainable parameters
rows.operation_detail: Derive asymptotic normalized regret as embedding width grows under subcritical Zipf marginals.
rows.measure: Expected normalized regret; theoretical capacity-bias term B and finite-sample term V
rows.value: r_{n,d}(N)≃B+V; B≃A if N=o(d), and B≃A(1−α)ψ/ρ if N≍d, where ψ=N/d and ψ=∫₀¹ρ/(ρ+t^α)dt; V≃(1−A)d/n for N=o(d), or (1−A)(1−ψ)d/n for N≍d
rows.note: An analytic result for the toy model’s normalized regret, not held-out cross-entropy.
rows.check: Link is correct. Note that for natural-language-like α<1 with sublinear width, B≃A: regret does not decay with N at all, so this is not a power law. Also, ψ=∫ρ/(ρ+t^α)dt defines ρ, not ψ itself; it is rendered ambiguously.
